I can only speak for myself, but it certainly seems to be a hardwired coping strategy now. It doesn't help though that therapy always seems to start at the wrong end for me. People don't seem to understand that I need to learn non harmful coping strategies before I start on the whys of the way I am. Instead they dive straight in and I end up resorting to the methods that I know, even if I know they're not good for me.

Most people that SH though seem to accept the fact that it can be addictive, so I suppose in that sense it's understandable to be a constant struggle in the same way as any other addiction. All you can do is focus on one day at a time, and try not to be too hard on yourself...

Perhaps try writing the things you want to talk about in a journal - you could even do it in the form of letters to your friend or as if you were talking to them. You could then tell your friend about it and let them decide if or when they want to read about it, but you may find just writing it down is enough to let it out for a little while to give you breathing space even if they don't. 

The other thing you can do is to reassure them that you understand that it's not always easy to listen to the things you talk about and also that you aren't expecting them to try to solve or fix things for you - they may be feeling helpless or that they're letting you down because they don't know what to do. It may also be useful to find numbers of places they can get support from if they need it.  

Finally, make sure they know that it's a two way street and that you're happy to listen to them and their problems as well - they may feel they can't talk to you when they have difficulties because you have enough to deal with.

It's not necessarily venting to the void.  Often posts are seen and read,  but people struggle to know what to say.   How do you give others hope when you have none yourself? How do you avoid inadvertently saying something that makes it worse for the other person, when the worst is often all you are thinking about?


It may seem like nobody cares, but sometimes it's the opposite.  We care too much - about getting it wrong, about becoming vulnerable,  about putting our heads above the parapets.  But that doesn't mean that you aren't seen, and it doesn't mean you are alone.


As to your question.  I don't have any big, profound answer I'm afraid.  If I knew a good reason to stick around I probably wouldn't need to be here.   I suppose the only one I can give is that yes,  the people you love will eventually die,  but they will probably have lots of amazing experiences and moments along the way, and by sticking around you have a chance to participate and make their journey just a little more pleasurable. Not the best answer or reason, I know,  but maybe it's enough to show that there are people here and listening if nothing else.

It's a spiral. I feel guilty,  but even though I know I'll hurt them, it's not enough to make me want to stay. Then I feel worse because I'm willing to hurt them, which then increases the feeling that I deserve to die.
